title: Transfer Pricing
subtitle: The arm's length principle - the Apple Ireland case
openingQuestion: What is transfer pricing inside a multinational group?
openingOptions: The internal price between related companies
A kind of short-term intra-group debt
explanation: Transfer pricing is the price affiliated companies use to sell goods, services or IP to one another. Because related parties have no incentive to bargain independently the way two strangers would, that price directly affects which country the profit - and the tax on it - is recognised in.

realWorldExample.company: Intellectual property - the hardest thing to price
realWorldExample.description: For physical goods, a tax authority can at least compare the internal price against the market price of a similar product. For intellectual property - a brand, a technology, an algorithm - that is far harder, because no reference market exists. A group can place the entity holding the IP wherever tax is low, and have subsidiaries in high-tax markets pay royalties back to it. In form, every transaction has a contract; in substance, the profit has moved away from where the revenue was actually earned. This is why transfer pricing rules focus hardest on intangibles and intra-group services.

sections.text: Inside a multinational group, subsidiaries constantly buy and sell goods, services or intellectual property from one another - and the price of those internal transactions has its own name: transfer pricing.
Why transfer pricing is watched so closely

Because related parties have no incentive to bargain independently the way two strangers would, the internal price can be adjusted to gather profit in whichever country taxes it least - an artificial form of tax optimisation. The arm's length principle requires internal transactions to be priced as though they were between two independent parties, so that profit, and tax, is recognised where the value was actually created.

items: Transfer pricing is the internal price between affiliated companies within one group
The arm's length principle requires internal pricing as if between two independent parties
Tax authorities watch it closely because distorted pricing can shift profit to a low-tax country artificially

sections.text: How the arm's length principle is tested

items: Comparable uncontrolled price: find a similar transaction between two unrelated parties and compare directly. The simplest method, but usually there is no suitable comparable data.
Resale price: take the price charged to the end customer and deduct a reasonable gross margin for the distribution step.
Cost plus: take the production cost and add the margin normal for the industry.
Transactional net margin and profit split: used when the methods above cannot be applied, especially for intangibles.

sections.label: Why an investor should care
sections.text: Transfer pricing risk is not a question of ethics but of cash flow: one reassessment by a tax authority can create an obligation in the hundreds of billions and years of dispute. For a company with large related-party transactions, the related-party note is the section to read carefully.

left.label: Signs to examine
left.text: The margin of the company in its largest market being unusually low against the group average; royalties or management fees paid to the parent making up a large share and growing faster than revenue.

right.label: Normal signs
right.text: Related-party transactions with complete pricing documentation, margins at each step in line with the industry, and notes that state which pricing method is being applied.

lines: Transfer pricing is not merely an internal accounting matter.
It directly affects where a group's profit is recognised - and taxed.

quiz.question: What is the arm's length principle for?
options: Exempting a group from preparing consolidated statements
Pricing internally as two independent parties would
Pushing profit to wherever the tax rate is lowest
Raising the share of fixed costs within cost of goods sold
quiz.explanation: Arm's length requires an internal transaction to look like a transaction between two independent parties.

quiz.question: Why are tax authorities so concerned with multinationals' transfer pricing?
options: Because transfer pricing applies only to large technology companies
Because international accounting rules forbid all transactions between related parties
Because distorted pricing can shift profit to a low-tax country
Because they want to control the quality of internally traded products
quiz.explanation: If a subsidiary in a high-tax country sells cheaply to one in a low-tax country - or is charged high fees for internal services or IP - group profit can be gathered artificially where tax is lowest. That is why tax authorities insist on the arm's length principle.

quiz.question: Why is internal IP harder to police for transfer pricing than physical goods?
options: Because tax authorities take no interest at all in internal intangibles
Because intangible assets may not be transferred within a group at all
Because intangible assets carry no value at all in the accounting records
Because there is no comparable market transaction to price against
quiz.explanation: The arm's length principle depends on finding a comparable transaction. For a brand or a proprietary technology no reference market exists, so the range of a 'reasonable' price is very wide.

quiz.question: For an investor, what is the main risk from a transfer pricing issue?
options: Tax reassessments and the cost of a long dispute, hitting cash flow
Revenue being written down across every market at once
The company being forced to reconsolidate all of its subsidiaries again
The shares being compulsorily delisted under exchange rules
quiz.explanation: This is the quantifiable risk, and it is tracked through the related-party note together with whatever tax provisions the company has set aside.

quiz.question: How do tax authorities usually test whether an internal price is reasonable?
options: Against production cost plus a fixed margin laid down by statute somewhere
Against the price of a similar transaction between two independent parties
Against the price the group applied in the prior reporting period
Against the average tax rate of the countries involved
quiz.explanation: The arm's length principle requires the price to match what two unrelated parties would have agreed. The hardest case is when no comparable transaction exists - precisely the case for brands and patents transferred internally.

keyTakeaways: Transfer pricing affects both profit and tax
The arm's length principle is the governing standard
It has to be read alongside the group structure

summary.keyIdea: Transfer pricing affects both profit and tax
summary.commonMistake: Easily overlooked: the arm's length principle is the governing standard
summary.action: Read it alongside the group structure

application.title: In practice: transfer pricing
application.message: What does the arm's length principle in transfer pricing require between related parties?
application.secondary: Grasping this principle raises your professional financial analysis to a higher level.

practicePrompt.question: What does the arm's length principle in transfer pricing require between related parties?
options: Prices between group companies must match market prices
Subsidiaries may freely set a price of zero to avoid tax
The group must remit 100% of profit to its head office country
Subsidiaries are not permitted to trade goods with one another
practicePrompt.explanation: The arm's length principle is the global anti-avoidance standard: it requires intra-group transaction prices to reflect genuine independent market value.
